```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gstat)
library(terra)
library(tmap)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
heat <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1tZQU5NwZ3Z1lBtFbJTvM7clB1z0sXMI9", quiet = TRUE) |>
  distinct()
nc_outline <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1SNy838Q7f7rvL6TFLmIZm-sKyRO7Htjw", quiet = TRUE)
jan_temp <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1Mtc7SXpWAx-atL5u1aFUuZli0wTMVTcT", quiet = TRUE)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
rmse <- function(cv) sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2))
heat_df_key <- data.frame(x = st_coordinates(heat)[, 1], y = st_coordinates(heat)[, 2], value = heat$value)
```

This tutorial runs over two class days. Day 1 covers inverse distance weighting (IDW) and Day 2 covers ordinary kriging. Each day has its own walkthrough, partner practice and index card.

## Day 1 Walkthrough: Inverse Distance Weighting {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in the Day 1 partner practice.

### Step 1: Load and Map the Data

::: {.why}
We'll use air temperatures (°F) at `r nrow(heat)` weather stations across North Carolina during the July 30, 2025 heat wave, from the [North Carolina State Climate Office](https://products.climate.ncsu.edu/cardinal/user/). Temperature exists everywhere, but we only measured it at these points. Interpolation predicts it everywhere else. Both files are in NC State Plane, so distances are in feet.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(gstat)
library(terra)
library(tmap)

#heat wave temperatures at weather stations
heat <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1tZQU5NwZ3Z1lBtFbJTvM7clB1z0sXMI9") |>
  distinct()

#North Carolina outline
nc_outline <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1SNy838Q7f7rvL6TFLmIZm-sKyRO7Htjw")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Map of weather stations across North Carolina colored by temperature during the July 30, 2025 heat wave, in five quantile classes with a legend. The coolest stations are in the western mountains, and most stations in the Piedmont and coastal plain are in the low to high 90s."}
tm_shape(nc_outline) + tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(heat) +
  tm_dots(fill = "value", size = 0.5,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-brewer.rd_yl_bu"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Temperature (°F)"))
```

### Step 2: Set Up the Data and the Grid

::: {.why}
`gstat` works with a plain table of x, y and the value. The prediction grid is an empty raster over North Carolina. A cell size of 10,000 feet (about 2 miles) is fine enough for a statewide map.
:::

```{r}
#table of coordinates and values
heat_df <- data.frame(x = st_coordinates(heat)[, 1],
                      y = st_coordinates(heat)[, 2],
                      value = heat$value)

#empty raster covering North Carolina, 10,000 ft cells
grid <- rast(vect(nc_outline), resolution = 10000)
```

### Step 3: Interpolate with IDW

::: {.why}
IDW predicts each cell as a weighted average of the stations, with closer stations weighted more. The power (`idp`) sets how fast the weight falls with distance. A low power gives a smooth surface, and a high power lets each station dominate its own area.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Map of the IDW temperature surface for North Carolina with power 2, with a legend. Temperatures are lowest in the western mountains and highest across the eastern Piedmont and coastal plain, with small bullseye spots around individual stations."}
idw_model <- gstat(formula = value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df,
                   set = list(idp = 2))

heat_idw <- interpolate(grid, idw_model, debug.level = 0)
heat_idw <- mask(heat_idw, vect(nc_outline))

tm_shape(heat_idw[["var1.pred"]]) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-brewer.rd_yl_bu"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted temperature (°F)"))
```

### Step 4: Choose the Power with Cross-Validation

::: {.why}
Leave-one-out cross-validation leaves out each station in turn, predicts it from the others, and records the error. The root mean square error (RMSE) summarizes the errors in °F. A lower RMSE is better.
:::

```{r}
#leave-one-out cross-validation for three powers
for (p in c(1, 2, 3)) {
  cv <- krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df,
                 set = list(idp = p), verbose = FALSE)
  print(paste("idp", p, "RMSE", round(sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2)), 2)))
}
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
heat_rmse <- sapply(c(1, 2, 3), function(p) rmse(krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df_key, set = list(idp = p), verbose = FALSE)))
```

The RMSE is `r fmt(heat_rmse[1])`°F for power 1, `r fmt(heat_rmse[2])`°F for power 2 and `r fmt(heat_rmse[3])`°F for power 3, so power 2 predicts the stations best.

## Day 2 Walkthrough: Ordinary Kriging {#walkthrough-2}

Use `heat_df`, `grid` and `nc_outline` from Day 1.

### Step 1: Experimental Variogram

::: {.why}
The variogram shows how different two stations' values are, on average, as the distance between them grows. The nugget is the difference at almost no distance, the sill is where the curve levels off, and the range is the distance where it levels off. Beyond the range, stations are no longer related.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Experimental variogram of heat wave temperatures. Semivariance rises quickly over the first 100,000 to 150,000 feet and then levels off at about 17."}
heat_vgm <- variogram(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df)
plot(heat_vgm)
```

### Step 2: Fit a Variogram Model Automatically

::: {.why}
`fit.variogram()` fits a curve to the variogram. Given a list of model shapes, it fits each one and keeps the best. Here we let it choose among spherical (`"Sph"`), exponential (`"Exp"`) and Gaussian (`"Gau"`).
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Experimental variogram of heat wave temperatures with the fitted spherical model drawn as a line through the points, with a nugget of about 7, a sill near 17 and a range of about 137,000 feet."}
heat_fit <- fit.variogram(heat_vgm, vgm(c("Sph", "Exp", "Gau")))
heat_fit
plot(heat_vgm, heat_fit)
```

### Step 3: Krige and Map the Prediction and Variance

::: {.why}
Kriging uses the fitted variogram to weight the stations. It also gives a kriging variance for every cell, which is a measure of uncertainty: it is low near stations and high far from them.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = c("Map of the kriging prediction of heat wave temperature for North Carolina, with a legend. Like the IDW surface, it is coolest in the western mountains and hottest in the east, but it is smoother, without bullseyes around stations.", "Map of kriging variance for North Carolina, with a legend. Variance is lowest near clusters of stations and highest along the coast and in gaps between stations, such as the far northeast.")}
krige_model <- gstat(formula = value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df,
                     model = heat_fit)

heat_krige <- interpolate(grid, krige_model, debug.level = 0)
heat_krige <- mask(heat_krige, vect(nc_outline))

tm_shape(heat_krige[["var1.pred"]]) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-brewer.rd_yl_bu"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted temperature (°F)"))

tm_shape(heat_krige[["var1.var"]]) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.purples"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Kriging variance"))
```

### Step 4: Compare with IDW

```{r}
krige_cv <- krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df,
                     model = heat_fit, verbose = FALSE)
sqrt(mean(krige_cv$residual^2))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
heat_fit_key <- fit.variogram(variogram(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df_key), vgm(c("Sph", "Exp", "Gau")))
heat_krige_rmse <- rmse(krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = heat_df_key, model = heat_fit_key, verbose = FALSE))
```

Kriging's RMSE is `r fmt(heat_krige_rmse)`°F, compared with `r fmt(heat_rmse[2])`°F for IDW with power 2. With this many stations the two are close, and kriging adds a map of where its predictions are least certain.

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
jan_df <- data.frame(x = st_coordinates(jan_temp)[, 1], y = st_coordinates(jan_temp)[, 2], value = jan_temp$value)
jan_idw <- sapply(c(1, 3), function(p) rmse(krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df, set = list(idp = p), verbose = FALSE)))
jan_vgm <- variogram(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df)
fit_sph <- fit.variogram(jan_vgm, vgm("Sph"))
fit_exp <- fit.variogram(jan_vgm, vgm("Exp"))
sph_rmse <- rmse(krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df, model = fit_sph, verbose = FALSE))
exp_rmse <- rmse(krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df, model = fit_exp, verbose = FALSE))
fit_auto <- fit.variogram(jan_vgm, vgm(c("Sph", "Exp")))
par_txt <- function(f) c(fmt(f$psill[1]), fmt(sum(f$psill)), fmt(f$range[2], 0))
```

### Day 1

| Power | RMSE (°F) | Smoother or more local? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `r fmt(jan_idw[1])` | Smoother, with values pulled toward the statewide average |
| 3 | `r fmt(jan_idw[2])` | More local, with bullseyes around stations |

Power 3 has the lower RMSE, so it predicts the stations better, even though its map looks patchier. The predictions are least trustworthy far from any station, such as the Outer Banks, the far northeast and parts of the mountains, where a single distant station decides the value.

### Day 2

| Method | Nugget | Sill | Range (feet) | RMSE (°F) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kriging, spherical | `r par_txt(fit_sph)[1]` | `r par_txt(fit_sph)[2]` | `r par_txt(fit_sph)[3]` | `r fmt(sph_rmse)` |
| Kriging, exponential | `r par_txt(fit_exp)[1]` | `r par_txt(fit_exp)[2]` | `r par_txt(fit_exp)[3]` | `r fmt(exp_rmse)` |
| IDW, power 3 | | | | `r fmt(jan_idw[2])` |

Your fitted values can differ a little if `fit.variogram()` starts from different values. Given both shapes, `fit.variogram()` picks the `r as.character(fit_auto$model[2])` model. The exponential model and IDW with power 3 are nearly tied, and both beat the spherical model. Kriging adds the variance map, which is highest in the gaps between stations and along the edges of the state, such as the coast and the far west. A good card recommends the exponential kriging surface (or IDW with power 3 if they prefer its simplicity) and names one of those areas as least certain.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
jan_temp <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1Mtc7SXpWAx-atL5u1aFUuZli0wTMVTcT")

#### Day 1, both partners ####
tm_shape(nc_outline) + tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(jan_temp) +
  tm_dots(fill = "value", size = 0.5,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-brewer.rd_yl_bu"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "January average high (°F)"))

jan_df <- data.frame(x = st_coordinates(jan_temp)[, 1],
                     y = st_coordinates(jan_temp)[, 2],
                     value = jan_temp$value)
grid <- rast(vect(nc_outline), resolution = 10000)

#Partner A uses idp = 1, Partner B uses idp = 3
jan_idw <- interpolate(grid, gstat(formula = value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df,
                                   set = list(idp = 1)), debug.level = 0)
jan_idw <- mask(jan_idw, vect(nc_outline))
tm_shape(jan_idw[["var1.pred"]]) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-brewer.rd_yl_bu"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted January high (°F)"))

cv <- krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df, set = list(idp = 1), verbose = FALSE)
sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2))

#### Day 2, both partners ####
jan_vgm <- variogram(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df)
plot(jan_vgm)

#Partner A uses "Sph", Partner B uses "Exp"
jan_fit <- fit.variogram(jan_vgm, vgm("Sph"))
jan_fit
plot(jan_vgm, jan_fit)

jan_krige <- interpolate(grid, gstat(formula = value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df,
                                     model = jan_fit), debug.level = 0)
jan_krige <- mask(jan_krige, vect(nc_outline))

tm_shape(jan_krige[["var1.pred"]]) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-brewer.rd_yl_bu"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Predicted January high (°F)"))
tm_shape(jan_krige[["var1.var"]]) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.purples"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Kriging variance"))

cv <- krige.cv(value ~ 1, locations = ~x + y, data = jan_df, model = jan_fit, verbose = FALSE)
sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2))
```
